<section class="page-hero"><h1>Sakya Monastery</h1><p class="lead">ས་སྐྱ་དགོན་པ་ · Sakya, Tsang, Tibet</p></section>
<main class="content"><div class="content-inner fieldwork-story">
<figure class="fieldwork-hero"><img src="/assets/images/sakya-02.jpg" alt="At Sakya Monastery" loading="eager"><figcaption>In front of Sakya Monastery after arriving in Tsang.</figcaption></figure>
<p class="lead">I came to Sakya because its name appears constantly whenever I work on thirteenth-century Tibetan Buddhism, Mongol religious politics, and the movement of ritual forms across Asia. In books, Sakya is an institution. On site, my first impression was far more physical: a massive complex of dark red, white and blue-grey walls rising in the high-altitude landscape, almost military in silhouette.</p>
<p>The monastery stands in Tsang, west of Shigatse. Sakya tradition dates its foundation to 1073, when Khön Könchok Gyalpo established the first centre of what became the Sakya school. Entering the courtyard, I understood how misleading photographs can be: they record the colours but not the weight of the architecture. Thick walls, relatively blind façades and compact volumes give the complex the presence of a fortress.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-03.jpg" alt="Courtyard of Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The courtyard and massive façades of Sakya.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This architecture interested me because it makes political history visible. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries Sakya was far more than a monastery. Sakya Paṇḍita's relationship with the Mongols, followed by that of his nephew ’Phags-pa with Qubilai, placed Sakya hierarchs at the centre of the Yuan imperial system. It is too simple to describe this as “Tibet ruled by Sakya monks”: authority was distributed among Mongol rulers, religious hierarchs and civil administrators. Walking through Sakya nevertheless gives a concrete sense of the institutional scale the monastery had acquired.</p>
<p>For me, Sakya was especially important because my work on Koryŏ led directly back to this world. From the second half of the thirteenth century, the Koryŏ court became increasingly integrated into the Yuan imperial sphere. What moved through that relationship was not only political institutions: Tibetan Buddhist teachers, texts, ritual objects, iconographic models and practices also reached the peninsula. Under Wŏnjong and especially Ch’ungnyŏl these forms became increasingly visible at court. Korean sources record, in 1294, the return of a monk from Koryŏ who had trained in Tibetan Buddhism and brought texts and ritual objects with him; early fourteenth-century records also note further arrivals of Tibetan scriptures. Visiting Sakya therefore allowed me to move back toward one of the intellectual and institutional centres that makes those changes intelligible. What I had been studying in Korea as traces, borrowings and transformations acquired a concrete historical setting here.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-01.jpg" alt="Assembly hall at Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Inside the great halls, the quality of light completely changes the experience of the architecture.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The transition from the courtyard to the interior was one of the strongest moments of my visit. Outside everything feels mineral and monumental. Inside, light becomes scarce, colours deepen and statues gradually emerge from darkness. I spent time looking not only at the images themselves but at the way they are installed among textiles, offerings, lamps and smaller figures. In a museum we often isolate an artwork. Here the image is never alone.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-04.jpg" alt="Buddha image at Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>A Buddha image still fully embedded in a ritual environment.</figcaption></figure>
<p>This difference matters for art history. Gilded bronzes, clay sculptures, paintings and altars can be studied through style, iconography and dating, but Sakya constantly brought me back to function. Traces of devotion, textiles, offerings and successive alterations show that these objects continue to be activated through religious practice. What I photographed was therefore not simply heritage, but a living religious environment.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-05.jpg" alt="’Phags-pa between Činggis Qan and Qubilai Qan at Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>’Phags-pa in the centre, flanked by Činggis Qan and Qubilai Qan. For me, this image makes the relationship between Sakya religious authority and Mongol imperial power immediately visible.</figcaption></figure>
<p>I spent a long time in front of this group. Seeing ’Phags-pa positioned between Činggis Qan and Qubilai Qan gives visual form to a relationship between religious master and ruler that political diagrams tend to flatten. This is precisely what matters for my work on Koryŏ: the peninsula did not simply receive an undifferentiated “Mongol Buddhism”, but religious forms shaped through the interaction of Tibetan hierarchs and imperial power. The group therefore gave me a visual bridge between Sakya and the transformations I study in late Koryŏ court Buddhism.</p>
<p>The library was probably the space that impressed me most intellectually. High wooden shelves are packed with wrapped volumes, stacked so high that one has to tilt one's head back to take in the whole wall. Sakya preserves one of Tibet's major textual collections, including canonical corpora and many ancient manuscripts. Travel writing and popular accounts sometimes call it a “second Dunhuang”. The comparison is dramatic and should be used cautiously, but it conveys something of the scale of the collection.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-06.jpg" alt="Library of Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The shelves of Sakya's library: text becoming architecture.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Standing in front of those shelves, I thought above all about the material chain of transmission. A Buddhist text is not an abstraction: it has to be copied, translated, corrected, printed, transported, preserved and read. For understanding religious circulation between Tibet, China and Koryŏ, these material objects matter as much as the doctrines they transmit.</p>
<figure><img src="/assets/images/sakya-07.jpg" alt="Stupas and altars inside Sakya Monastery" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Stupas, images and ritual objects create a space in which architecture and devotion are inseparable.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Another aspect of Sakya that interested me was the coexistence of institutional Buddhism and local traditions. A small rooftop shrine is sometimes described locally as the “Chapel of the Witches”. Tradition says it was used to subdue harmful female spirits or sorceresses. I prefer to preserve this as a tradition rather than turn it into a historical fact. Even so, it is revealing of the way Tibetan sacred landscapes absorb narratives of protection, subjugation and the control of local forces.</p>
<p>I left Sakya thinking less of an isolated monument than of a node: between study and devotion, architecture and political power, material culture and textual transmission, Tibetan history and wider Eurasian networks. That is why the visit mattered to me. It gave scale, light and material presence to historical processes that can become too abstract when encountered only through texts.</p>
<div class="fieldwork-notes"><h2>Reference points</h2><p><strong>Foundation:</strong> 1073, traditionally attributed to Khön Könchok Gyalpo.<br><strong>Location:</strong> Sakya, Tsang, Shigatse region.<br><strong>Coordinates:</strong> approx. 28.905° N, 88.018° E.<br><strong>Tradition:</strong> Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism.</p></div>
</div></main>
